items.stem: A finance-ops team's nightly reconciliation job runs unattended in a cron container, fetches related ledger entries mid-analysis to confirm each anomaly, and feeds a pipeline that pages on-call by severity. One malformed record broke a night's paging. Which mechanism fits the requirement?

opts.t: Add `-p` (`--print`) so the job runs non-interactively instead of waiting on stdin.
Run with `--output-format json` and enforce `--json-schema` so every finding carries a guaranteed, parseable shape.
Move the job to the Batch API, since nobody is waiting and it costs half as much.
Add a detailed 'Output Format' section to the project's CLAUDE.md describing the exact JSON shape every finding must follow.

items.whyRight: `--output-format json` combined with `--json-schema` guarantees every finding carries a well-formed, parseable shape on every run, which the downstream pipeline's severity-based paging depends on; a nightly cron schedule and a mid-analysis ledger lookup do not change that requirement.

whyWrong.A: Running non-interactively stops the job from hanging on stdin, but says nothing about whether each finding's fields are well-formed enough for the pipeline to parse.
whyWrong.C: The job fetches related ledger entries mid-analysis, and the Batch API cannot execute a tool mid-request and return the result, disqualifying it regardless of the flexible deadline.
whyWrong.D: A CLAUDE.md description raises the odds of a well-formed record but never guarantees one; the parser still fails on the first run that deviates from the description.

items.t1Clause: The stem states the job 'feeds a pipeline that pages on-call by severity' and 'One malformed record broke a night's paging' — the evidence that forces a guaranteed schema. Invert by deleting that consumer and the malformed-record evidence entirely, leaving only 'runs unattended in a cron container' as the operative fact, which correctly justifies option A's non-interactive `-p` fix instead.

items.stem: A clinical-operations agent must never export patient identifiers outside the de-identified pipeline, regardless of prompt wording, and every export it does run must post an entry to the compliance audit log automatically. Which two configuration changes guarantee both? Select two.

opts.t: Add a strongly-worded instruction to the project CLAUDE.md forbidding identifier exports and reminding the agent to log every export.
Escalate both rules to managed enterprise policy settings, even though only this one agent's configuration is affected.
Add a `deny` rule for the identifier-export command pattern to `settings.json` permissions.
Add a hook, scoped to export events by `matcher`, that writes the audit-log entry automatically.

items.whyRight: A `deny` rule blocks the export outside model discretion regardless of prompt wording, and a hook scoped to export events writes the audit-log entry every time one fires — both are enforced by Claude Code itself, independent of what any instruction asks the agent to do.

whyWrong.A: A CLAUDE.md instruction shapes what the agent tries to do; it does not change what Claude Code allows, so a determined or malformed prompt can still trigger the export.
whyWrong.B: Managed policy fits a rule that must survive every local override across many machines; escalating one agent's rule there is more governance than a single agent's configuration needs.

items.t1Clause: The stem scopes the requirement to 'a clinical-operations agent's configuration' — one agent's own settings.json. Invert by making it a rule that must hold across every developer machine and survive local overrides, which correctly justifies option B's managed-policy escalation instead of a single agent's settings.json deny.
items.lessonKey: deny event hook json matcher permissions relevant rule scoped settings
items.factAnswerRaw: A `deny` rule in `settings.json` permissions; A hook on the relevant event, scoped by matcher

items.stem: A twelve-engineer team's masking convention has always reached everyone. This week a new engineer's code omits it, the same day a teammate merges an unrelated rules file. The other eleven still see it; root `CLAUDE.md` is unchanged. What should the team check first?

opts.t: Revert the unrelated rules-file merge, since it landed the same day the symptom appeared.
Run `/context` in the new engineer's session, since the convention may live only in the other engineers' personal configuration.
Have the new engineer restate the convention in every prompt until someone fixes it properly.
Post the convention in the onboarding channel and link it from the new-hire welcome email.

items.whyRight: The masking convention has always reached everyone, so the coincidental same-day rules-file merge is not the cause; root `CLAUDE.md` is unchanged, meaning the convention was never centralized there. `/context` shows what the new engineer's session actually loaded, confirming whether it is missing entirely.

whyWrong.A: Reverting the merge treats same-day timing as causal, but root `CLAUDE.md` is unchanged and the merge scopes an unrelated rule — the coincidence explains nothing.
whyWrong.C: Restating the convention per prompt patches each session downstream of a configuration gap `/context` would locate, and fails silently the moment someone forgets.
whyWrong.D: Posting to a channel transfers the knowledge to a human, not to the model's own request, and does not explain why only the new engineer lacks it.

items.t1Clause: The stem pins 'root `CLAUDE.md` is unchanged' to rule out the coincidental merge. Invert by removing that pinned fact, which reopens the same-day merge as a live suspect and correctly justifies option A's revert instead.
items.lessonKey: configuration context convention engineer engineers live new other personal run s session
items.factAnswerRaw: Run `/context` in the new engineer's session, since the convention may live only in the other engineers' personal configuration.
